title: How Crystals Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain what crystals are: repeating three-dimensional atomic structures built from unit cells into lattices, not just a type of mineral or gem. They cover the seven lattice shapes, long- versus short-range order, and polycrystals versus single crystals. They describe three ways crystals form (from solution, from vapor, from melt) with home salt-crystal experiments, and human-made methods such as Czochralski crystal pulling, Bridgman-Stockbarger, molecular beam and chemical vapor deposition, and liquid phase epitaxy. They discuss gemstone colors from impurities (ruby vs. sapphire, amethyst vs. citrine), the Greek origin of the word crystal, and the Cueva de los Cristales. The episode closes with crystal healing and its placebo basis (including a University of London study), the risks of Baltic amber teething necklaces, and listener mail about the origin of the word nickname.

segments.title: Opening banter and what makes crystals special
segments.summary: The hosts introduce crystals as the most ordered structure, with a repeating atomic pattern. They discuss the word crystallize, common misconceptions about crystals, and the seven lattice shapes. Josh plugs his live shows and the End of the World series.

segments.title: Crystal structure, unit cells and lattices
segments.summary: Crystals are repeating three-dimensional atomic arrangements, not a type of object. Ions attract and clump into unit cells that build into a lattice. The hosts describe long-range and short-range order, with liquid crystals as an example of short-range order.

segments.title: Polycrystals, single crystals and strength
segments.summary: Gemstones are usually single crystals formed under ideal conditions, which are rare. Most natural material is polycrystalline, made of many crystals grown together. Polycrystals are generally not stronger than single crystals because their joints are weak points.

segments.title: Growing crystals at home and from solution
segments.summary: The hosts describe a home experiment growing salt crystals from a saturated hot salt solution on a string. They explain that cooling reduces the space between molecules, pushing dissolved solute into solid crystals, which can also occur underwater, in magma and in clouds.

segments.title: Vapor deposition and snowflakes
segments.summary: Crystals can also form from supersaturated gas through vapor deposition, the process that forms snowflakes. Solution growth is faster and can produce bigger crystals.

segments.title: Growth from melt and crystal pulling
segments.summary: Growth from melt cools a liquid until it crystallizes. The hosts describe the Czochralski crystal pulling method, named for a Polish scientist, in which a seed crystal is dipped into molten material and slowly raised. Modern automation yields very large, pure crystals, such as silicon.

segments.title: Bridgman-Stockbarger method and epitaxy
segments.summary: The Bridgman-Stockbarger method cools molten material in a cone-shaped tube from the tip upward to grow one large crystal. The hosts then cover epitaxy methods: molecular beam epitaxy, which is considered the best human-made method, chemical vapor deposition (used for synthetic diamonds), and liquid phase epitaxy.

segments.title: Diamond trade names and personal aside
segments.summary: The hosts recall the nineties trade names diamonique, diamonoid, and cubic zirconia. Josh describes visiting the Smithsonian's Museum of Natural History to see its crystal and gem collection, including fluorescent minerals under black light.

segments.title: Gem colors, graphite vs diamond, and crystal names
segments.summary: Impurities give gemstones their color: chromium makes rubies red, while iron and titanium make sapphires blue. The word crystal comes from the Greek krystallos, meaning ice. Amethyst and citrine are both quartz, differing by formation conditions. Diamonds can slowly turn into graphite over time.

segments.title: Crystal shapes, the Cueva de los Cristales, and growth rates
segments.summary: Crystals can form other shapes such as plates, tables, and needles under nonideal conditions. The hosts mention the Cueva de los Cristales in Chihuahua, Mexico. Garnet can take ten million years to grow two centimeters.

segments.title: Crystal healing and the placebo effect
segments.summary: The hosts describe crystal healing, which places stones on chakra points, and note there is no scientific evidence for it or for ancient use. A University of London study found that people holding fake crystals reported the same effects as those holding real ones, and primed participants reported stronger effects, suggesting placebo. The hosts note that crystal healers are not licensed.

segments.title: Baltic amber teething necklaces
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the belief that Baltic amber necklaces relieve teething. Succinic acid is said to be released by body heat, but this has not been shown. The necklaces pose choking and safety risks.

segments.title: Carrying crystals and closing remarks
segments.summary: Chuck recalls carrying a crystal in his pocket as a fidget object rather than for energy. The hosts end the crystal discussion and advise not to skip medical care.

segments.title: Listener mail: origin of the word nickname
segments.summary: Liz writes about the origin of nickname, which comes from Middle English ekename, meaning additional name, rather than from Nicholas. She also shares that her twins are due in June and that she and her husband Nick are expecting. The hosts sign off.
